summary.text: Using \(\sum_{j\ge0}\lfloor e/2^j\rfloor=2e-s_2(e)\), the proof identifies the prime-power generating series with \(\prod_{i\ge0}(1+2^{2^{i+1}-1}x^{2^i})\). For \(k=2^a m\) with \(m\) odd, the \(x^k\)-coefficient of half its logarithmic derivative is nonnegative because its single positive \(i=a\) term dominates the sum of the negative \(i<a\) terms by a geometric bound; the resulting coefficient recurrence makes the square-root series nonnegative, and multiplicativity lifts this from prime powers to all integers.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
S(e)=\sum_{j\ge 0}\left\lfloor \frac e{2^j}\right\rfloor.
\]
Only finitely many summands are nonzero. This is the function denoted A005187 in the definition of A046644. We will first rewrite it in terms of binary digits.

Define \(s_2(e)\) to be the number of 1's in the binary expansion of \(e\). Equivalently,
\[
s_2(0)=0,\qquad s_2(e)=s_2(\lfloor e/2\rfloor)+(e\bmod 2)\quad(e>0).
\]
Separating the \(j=0\) term in the sum defining \(S\), and replacing \(j+1\) by \(j\) in all the other terms, gives
\[
S(e)=e+S(\lfloor e/2\rfloor).
\]
We claim that
\[
S(e)=2e-s_2(e). \tag{1}
\]
This follows by strong induction on \(e\). It is clear for \(e=0\). For \(e>0\), write \(r=e\bmod 2\), so that
\(e=2\lfloor e/2\rfloor+r\), where \(r\in\{0,1\}\). By the induction hypothesis and the two recurrences above,
\[
\begin{aligned}
S(e)
 &=e+2\lfloor e/2\rfloor-s_2(\lfloor e/2\rfloor)\\
 &=2e-\bigl(s_2(\lfloor e/2\rfloor)+r\bigr)
 =2e-s_2(e).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus (1) holds.

For future use, note also that if \(0\le n<2^m\), then adding \(2^m\) adds a new leading binary 1 and causes no carry, so
\[
s_2(n+2^m)=s_2(n)+1. \tag{2}
\]

We now work with formal power series over \(\mathbb Q\). Put
\[
c_i=2^{2^{i+1}-1},\qquad P_i(x)=1+c_i x^{2^i}\quad(i\ge0).
\]
For \(m\ge0\), let
\[
P^{(m)}(x)=\prod_{i=0}^{m-1}P_i(x),
\]
with the empty product equal to 1. Define
\[
A_e=2^{2e-s_2(e)}. \tag{3}
\]
We claim that, for \(e<2^m\), the coefficient of \(x^e\) in \(P^{(m)}\) is \(A_e\), and all coefficients in degrees at least \(2^m\) are zero.

This may be seen directly from binary expansion, or inductively. It is true for \(m=0\). Passing from \(m\) to \(m+1\) multiplies by \(1+c_mx^{2^m}\). Thus the lower block of coefficients, in degrees \(0,\ldots,2^m-1\), is unchanged, while the upper block, in degrees \(2^m,\ldots,2^{m+1}-1\), is the lower block multiplied by \(c_m\). If \(e<2^m\), then by (2),
\[
\begin{aligned}
A_{e+2^m}
 &=2^{2(e+2^m)-s_2(e+2^m)}\\
 &=2^{2e-s_2(e)}\,2^{2^{m+1}-1}
 =A_e c_m.
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves the assertion. Consequently the coefficientwise meaningful infinite product
\[
A(x)=\prod_{i\ge0}P_i(x)
\]
has coefficient sequence \((A_e)_{e\ge0}\): only factors with \(2^i\le e\) can affect the coefficient of degree \(e\).

The next step is to study the logarithmic derivative of this product. For each \(i\), define a formal power series
\[
Q_i(x)=\sum_{r\ge1}(-1)^{r-1}c_i^r2^i x^{r2^i}. \tag{4}
\]
Since
\[
\frac1{1+c_ix^{2^i}}=\sum_{r\ge0}(-1)^r c_i^r x^{r2^i},
\]
we have the formal identity
\[
xP_i'(x)=Q_i(x)P_i(x). \tag{5}
\]
Indeed, the left side is \(2^ic_ix^{2^i}\), while multiplication of the geometric series by \(1+c_ix^{2^i}\) cancels every term except the first one.

Let
\[
Q(x)=\sum_{i\ge0}Q_i(x).
\]
This sum is coefficientwise finite: the coefficient of \(x^k\) in \(Q_i\) is zero unless \(2^i\mid k\), and in particular it is zero when \(2^i>k>0\); every \(Q_i\) has zero constant term. Applying the product rule to a finite product and using (5) gives
\[
x(P^{(m)})'(x)=\left(\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}Q_i(x)\right)P^{(m)}(x). \tag{6}
\]
In each fixed degree, both sides stabilize as \(m\) grows. Therefore
\[
xA'(x)=Q(x)A(x). \tag{7}
\]

Write
\[
Q(x)=2\sum_{k\ge0}q_kx^k;
\]
thus \(q_0=0\), and \(q_k\) for \(k>0\) is one half of the coefficient of \(x^k\) in \(Q\). The crucial fact is
\[
q_k\ge0\qquad(k>0). \tag{8}
\]
We now prove this explicitly.

Fix \(k>0\), and write
\[
k=m_0 2^a,
\]
where \(a=v_2(k)\) and \(m_0\) is odd. In particular, \(m_0\ge1\). The coefficient of \(x^k\) in \(Q_i\) vanishes for \(i>a\). If \(i\le a\), formula (4), with \(r=k/2^i\), gives the coefficient
\[
(-1)^{k/2^i-1}c_i^{k/2^i}2^i.
\]
For \(i=a\), the quotient \(k/2^a=m_0\) is odd, so the sign is positive. For \(i<a\),
\[
\frac{k}{2^i}=m_0 2^{a-i}
\]
is even, so \(k/2^i-1\) is odd and the sign is negative. Hence
\[
2q_k=c_a^{m_0}2^a-
\sum_{i=0}^{a-1}c_i^{m_0 2^{a-i}}2^i. \tag{9}
\]
We must show that the positive term dominates the sum.

Since \(c_i=2^{2^{i+1}-1}\), the positive term in (9) is
\[
c_a^{m_0}2^a
=2^{m_0 2^{a+1}-m_0+a}. \tag{10}
\]
For \(i<a\), the corresponding positive magnitude in the sum is
\[
c_i^{m_0 2^{a-i}}2^i
=2^{m_0 2^{a+1}-m_0 2^{a-i}+i}. \tag{11}
\]
Set \(M=m_0 2^{a+1}\). Reflecting the index by putting \(i=a-1-j\), the sum of (11) becomes
\[
2^{M+a}\sum_{j=0}^{a-1}2^{-\left(j+1+m_0 2^{j+1}\right)}. \tag{12}
\]
Because \(2^{j+1}\ge2\),
\[
j+1+m_0 2^{j+1}\ge j+1+2m_0.
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{j=0}^{a-1}2^{-\left(j+1+m_0 2^{j+1}\right)}
&\le \sum_{j=0}^{a-1}2^{-(j+1+2m_0)}\\
&=2^{-2m_0}(1-2^{-a})\\
&\le 2^{-2m_0}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Using this in (12) shows
\[
\sum_{i=0}^{a-1}c_i^{m_0 2^{a-i}}2^i
\le 2^{M-2m_0+a}.
\]
Finally,
\[
M-2m_0+a\le M-m_0+a
\]
because \(m_0\ge1\). By (10), the right side of (9) is therefore nonnegative. This proves (8).

We now construct the desired square root at the level of exponent sequences. Define rational numbers \(F_n\) recursively by
\[
F_0=1,
\qquad
F_n=\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^n F_{n-k}q_k\quad(n>0). \tag{13}
\]
This uniquely defines \(F_n\), because every \(F_{n-k}\) on the right has smaller index. Moreover,
\[
F_n\ge0\quad\text{for every }n. \tag{14}
\]
Indeed, this follows by strong induction. The base value is 1. For \(n>0\), every \(F_{n-k}\) is nonnegative by induction, every \(q_k\) is nonnegative by (8), and division by the positive integer \(n\) preserves nonnegativity.

Let
\[
F(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}F_nx^n,
\qquad q(x)=\sum_{k\ge1}q_kx^k.
\]
The recursion (13) says coefficient by coefficient that
\[
xF'(x)=q(x)F(x). \tag{15}
\]
We will show that
\[
F(x)^2=A(x). \tag{16}
\]
One can derive this immediately by formal differentiation: (15) gives
\[
x(F^2)'=2F(xF')=2qF^2=QF^2,
\]
whereas (7) gives \(xA'=QA\), and both series have constant term 1. For completeness, here is the coefficientwise uniqueness argument that justifies the last conclusion without any division of formal series.

Let
\[
H_n=\sum_{j=0}^nF_jF_{n-j},
\]
the coefficient of \(x^n\) in \(F(x)^2\). From the differentiated identity above, or directly from (13) and the product rule, one obtains
\[
nH_n=\sum_{k=1}^n 2q_kH_{n-k}\quad(n>0). \tag{17}
\]
On the other hand, taking coefficients in (7), and using \(Q=2q\), gives
\[
nA_n=\sum_{k=1}^n2q_kA_{n-k}\quad(n>0). \tag{18}
\]
Also \(H_0=F_0^2=1=A_0\). Equations (17) and (18) force \(H_n=A_n\) by induction on \(n\): if equality is known below \(n\), the right sides agree, so \(nH_n=nA_n\), and \(n\ne0\) in \(\mathbb Q\). Thus (16) is proved, or equivalently
\[
\sum_{j=0}^eF_jF_{e-j}=A_e=2^{2e-s_2(e)}=2^{S(e)}. \tag{19}
\]

We now pass from sequences indexed by prime-power exponents to arithmetic functions. Given any sequence \(U_0,U_1,\ldots\) with \(U_0=1\), define, for \(n\ge1\),
\[
G_U(n)=\prod_{p}U_{v_p(n)}, \tag{20}
\]
where only primes dividing \(n\) contribute, and set \(G_U(0)=0\). This is a multiplicative arithmetic function: if \(r\) and \(s\) are coprime, then for each prime at most one of \(v_p(r),v_p(s)\) is nonzero, so (20) gives \(G_U(rs)=G_U(r)G_U(s)\). It also satisfies
\[
G_U(p^e)=U_e. \tag{21}
\]

The arithmetic function A046644 is defined for \(n\ge1\) by
\[
\operatorname{A046644}(n)=\prod_{p^e\parallel n}2^{S(e)}.
\]
By (1) and (3), this is exactly
\[
\operatorname{A046644}(n)=\prod_{p^e\parallel n}A_e=G_A(n). \tag{22}
\]

Let \(*\) now denote Dirichlet convolution. We claim
\[
G_F*G_F=G_A. \tag{23}
\]
It is enough to inspect prime powers and then use multiplicativity. At \(p^e\), whose divisors are \(1,p,\ldots,p^e\), equations (21) and (19) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
(G_F*G_F)(p^e)
&=\sum_{j=0}^eG_F(p^j)G_F(p^{e-j})\\
&=\sum_{j=0}^eF_jF_{e-j}
=A_e
=G_A(p^e).
\end{aligned}
\]
Both sides of (23) are multiplicative: \(G_A\) is multiplicative by construction, and the Dirichlet convolution of two multiplicative functions is multiplicative. Hence agreement at every prime power yields agreement at every positive integer. Combining (22) and (23),
\[
(G_F*G_F)(n)=\operatorname{A046644}(n)\qquad(n\ge1). \tag{24}
\]

Moreover, (14) immediately gives
\[
G_F(n)=\prod_{p^e\parallel n}F_e\ge0\qquad(n\ge1). \tag{25}
\]
It remains only to identify \(G_F\) with the recursively specified Dirichlet convolution square root used to define A317940.

Let \(f\) denote that recursively defined rational sequence. Thus
\[
f(0)=0,\qquad f(1)=1,
\]
and for \(n>1\),
\[
f(n)=\frac12\left(
\operatorname{A046644}(n)
-
\sum_{\substack{d\mid n\\1<d<n}}f(d)f(n/d)
\right). \tag{26}
\]
The function \(G_F\) satisfies exactly the same recurrence. Indeed, (24) says
\[
\operatorname{A046644}(n)
=\sum_{d\mid n}G_F(d)G_F(n/d).
\]
Since \(G_F(1)=F_0=1\), the terms corresponding to \(d=1\) and \(d=n\) are both \(G_F(n)\). Separating those two endpoint divisors gives, for \(n>1\),
\[
G_F(n)=\frac12\left(
\operatorname{A046644}(n)
-
\sum_{\substack{d\mid n\\1<d<n}}G_F(d)G_F(n/d)
\right). \tag{27}
\]

We prove \(f(n)=G_F(n)\) by strong induction on \(n\). It holds at \(0\) and \(1\). Suppose \(n>1\) and equality is known for all smaller arguments. For every divisor \(d\) with \(1<d<n\), both \(d<n\) and \(n/d<n\). Therefore the induction hypothesis replaces both occurrences of \(f\) in each summand of (26) by \(G_F\). Equations (26) and (27) then have identical right sides, proving
\[
f(n)=G_F(n)\quad\text{for every }n. \tag{28}
\]

Finally, if \(n\ge1\), equations (25) and (28) give
\[
f(n)\ge0.
\]
Thus the rational Dirichlet-convolution square root underlying A317940 is nonnegative at every positive integer. In particular, when \(f(n)\) is written in lowest terms with positive denominator, its numerator is nonnegative. Hence every term \(a(n)\) of A317940 is nonnegative for \(n\ge1\), as claimed.
